Understanding Backpressure in Streams

By Ada Example · March 14, 2026

TwitterLinkedInEmail

Backpressure is what happens when a producer of data is faster than its consumer. Without it, buffers grow until the process runs out of memory, as described in the Node.js guide.[1]

This post explains how streams signal backpressure, why ignoring the return value of write() is a common bug, and how to fix it with a few lines of code.

How streams signal pressure

Every writable stream has a high-water mark. When the internal buffer passes it, write() returns false and the producer should wait for the drain event before writing again.

A minimal example

1const ok = writable.write(chunk);
2if (!ok) {
3  await once(writable, "drain");
4}

Comparison of approaches

ApproachMemoryComplexity
Ignore return valueUnboundedLow
Wait for drainBoundedMedium
Use pipeline()BoundedLow
Checklist
  1. Check the return value of write().
  2. Prefer pipeline() for chains:
    • it forwards errors
    • it cleans up on failure
  3. Measure buffer sizes in production.

Backpressure is not an error. It is the system telling you the truth about its capacity.

The throughput of a pipeline is limited by its slowest stage: $T = \min_i r_i$.

[1] The guide also covers readable streams.
